idiom_name: UA/PA assignment tables + role hierarchy + session active-role set + per-role admin roles terminating in one root admin
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: hold four things as data, not code - a subject->roles relation (UA), a role->permissions relation (PA) where a permission is an operation-on-object pair, a partial order over roles (RH) for inheritance, and a session that carries the subset of a subject's assigned roles active right now. A protected operation is allowed iff the active role set, closed under RH, contains a role that PA maps to that permission, and denied otherwise; unknown roles, missing entries and lookup errors all resolve to deny (deny by default). Administration is itself modelled: each role names the admin roles allowed to grant or revoke it, the chain terminates in a root admin held by the smallest, hardest identity in the system (multisig, timelock, hardware-backed service account), and every assignment change writes a grant/revoke event that the audit trail consumes. Encode static separation-of-duty exclusions as data (pairs of roles no subject may hold together) and check them in the grant path; review the two matrices on a schedule and expire just-in-time grants. Every concrete realization below supplies the same four relations through framework primitives - roles from claims or a role store, and the check at one guard, middleware or annotation seam.
code_sketch:
UA: subjects x roles              PA: roles x permissions        RH: roles partial order
session(S) -> active_roles subset of UA[S], closed under RH
allow(s, op, obj) iff exists r in active_roles(S) : (r, (op,obj)) in PA
grant(admin, s, r) iff admin in admins_of(r)
# deny by default: empty active_roles / unknown role / lookup error -> deny
pitfalls: Attaching permissions directly to subjects instead of to roles (the group loophole) makes the matrix incomplete and unreviewable; permissions belong on roles only.
Testing assignment membership instead of the session's active set silently defeats dynamic separation of duties - a subject holding two conflicting roles passes every check.
Resolving the subject or its roles from request-supplied data rather than an authenticated identity lets a caller widen its own permissions; roles come from trusted session state only.
A root admin held by a hot deployer key or a single account concentrates all power; compromise is a full takeover - hold it in a multisig or timelocked transfer.
Role explosion by cloning (MINTER_V2, SUPER_MINTER) makes the matrix unauditable; prefer one role plus hierarchy, scoping or attributes.
